text:
In the Provincial Court of Alberta

Citation: R.
v. Kelley, 2006 ABPC 17

Date:

20060310

Docket:

A00572235Y

Registry:

Hinton

Between:

Her Majesty the Queen

-
and -

Kipp Kelley

Reasons
for Judgment of The
Honourable
Judge D.C. Norheim

[
1
]

The defendant is charged with
contravening section 24(1) of the
Wildlife Act
.
He admits that he
was trapping squirrels on his uncle's trapline and he was not licensed to do
so.

[
2
]

There are two lines of defence
that must be considered by the court. First, do the defendant’s constitutional
rights as a Métis provide him with the right to trap as he did. Second, does
the Interim Métis Harvesting Agreement (“IMHA”) provide the defendant with the
right do so.

[
3
]

The defendant has established that
he is a Métis, however, he has not established that he was exercising his
constitutional rights in trapping as he did.

[
4
]

The IMHA cannot operate as a
defence to this charge. To the extent that the IMHA conflicts with or extends
rights which have been granted under the
Constitution Act, 1982
, the
IMHA will have no effect.

EVIDENCE

[
5
]

The Crown called Wildlife Officer
Tony Brooks. He gave evidence that he had received a confidential complaint of
a suspicious vehicle parked on the Willow Creek Road approximately six
kilometers from Hinton. He attended at this location and observed a vehicle,
which he recognized as belonging to the defendant, parked alongside the road
adjacent to a pipeline that intersected the road. There was no one at the
vehicle and he observed, in the open truck box of the vehicle, a white plastic
bag which contained the parts of approximately 12 squirrels and one fresh
squirrel pelt. He also observed a number of snares and traps in the back of the
truck and a dead martin. The martin had not been skinned and was still warm.

[
6
]

The defendant approached the
vehicle while the officer was making these observations. A conversation took
place between them wherein the defendant advised that he was looking for
horses. He was asked about the trapping paraphernalia and denied that he was
trapping. He offered to show the officer where he had been, and when the
officer took him up on this offer, he indicated that he could not do it now but
would return in 40 minutes. The officer noted that at this point he seemed to
become nervous as he would not look at the officer.

[
7
]

After the defendant had left, the
officer followed his footprints in the snow and in the ground.  He followed the
tracks to a point about 30 meters from the road where he observed a fresh
martin set which contained the carcass of a squirrel placed behind a leg hold
trap.

[
8
]

The defendant subsequently gave a
statement to the officer acknowledging that he had been trapping squirrels. He
indicated that he had set the traps with his children to teach them how to
trap. Officer Brooks had some further contact with the defendant when he
approached the defendant to sign an Indian violation report taken in compliance
with the Interim Métis Harvesting Agreement. The officer also attended at a
later date to see if he could obtain a further statement and the defendant
declined to provide a statement at that time.

[
9
]

The officer indicated while he
knew the defendant, he did not know that he was a Métis. He did acknowledge
that he was aware that there were some Métis people living in the community.

[
10
]

The defendant gave evidence. He
indicated that on the day that he was observed by Officer Brooks, that he had
gone to that area to spring all the snares that he had set for squirrels. He
had set roughly 24 snares two or three days earlier with his children as he had
wanted them to see how their grandfather traps. As the children didn't want to
trap anymore, he decided to spring all the snares that he had set. The
defendant indicated he knew that the trapline belonged to Frank Hunt. Frank
Hunt is his uncle but he did not have permission to trap on this trapline. He
trapped there because he thought that Frank was not using the trapline.

[
11
]

The defendant gave evidence that
he considered himself to be Métis. His grandfather was Irish and his
grandmother was mostly native. His father's family had come to the Hinton area
in the 1940s. His mother's side came from Cardston. He indicates that he did
not, at the time of this incident, have a Métis card. He had earlier had one
but lost it. He obtained his original Métis card in approximately 1991 and had
used it to vote in one Métis election. He had lost it some time ago and never
bothered to have it replaced. After he was charged he applied for a further
Métis card which he hoped to receive shortly. His father and siblings have
Métis cards. He was born and raised in Hinton, and has a number of friends who
are Métis. He has approximately 40 cousins, uncles and aunts who live in the
area. He is married to a woman with aboriginal roots. In the summer and fall he
works for his father guiding. During the winter he is employed in the oil
patch. He indicated that he grew up hunting and trapping and wanted to teach
his children how to trap. He was trapping squirrels because they are easy to
trap. He gave evidence that he wasn't planning to sell the squirrels that he
trapped.

[
12
]

George Patrick Kelley gave
evidence. He is the father of the defendant, and a member of the Métis Nation
of Alberta. George Kelley's father was white and his mother was three-quarter
native. She was born in Barnett, Alberta in approximately 1908. Her family had
trapped in the area of Lac St. Anne. When George Kelley was a boy he spent much
of his time with his mother and father on the Berland River hunting and
trapping. The Berland River is approximately 60 miles north of the Town of Hinton.
His grandmother was born near the Red River in Manitoba. His father, mother and
uncles taught him how to hunt and trap. He had voted in Métis elections in the
’70s, ’80s and ’90s. The defendant was helping skin and stretch hides that
George had caught on a trapline that George has near Rock Lake, which is 40 or
50 miles from Hinton. He indicates that there are hundreds of Métis in Hinton.
Many are relatives and most of his family have Métis cards. He earns most of
his income from hunting and trapping.  Ninety-five percent of his income came
from outfitting and five percent came from trapping.

[
13
]

The defendant's sister, Karina
Gale Kelley, gave evidence. She indicates that she considers herself to be
Métis. She obtained her first Métis card in 1979 or ’81. She used to vote in
Métis elections in Edmonton but hasn't voted recently. It is her view that
there is a community of Métis people in Hinton.

[
14
]

When I consider all of the
evidence I am not satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant was
trapping for any other purpose except for what could be categorized as cultural
purposes in teaching his children how to trap. He has admitted that he was
trapping for this purpose. The facts establish that he was hunting without a
license. Hunting under the definition sections of the
Wildlife Act

includes trapping. I find the evidence given by the defendant, his father and
sister to be credible with reference to a family history with a trapping
background, and the defendant’s connection to a Métis community in Hinton.

LEGISLATION AND AGREEMENTS

[
15
]

The
Canadian Charter of Rights
and Freedoms
reads:

15.

(1)  Every individual is equal before
and under the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit
of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination
based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental
or physical disability.

[
16
]

Sections 1 and 2 of the
Alberta
Bill of Rights
reads as follows:

1.
It is hereby recognized and declared that in Alberta
there exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour,
religion or sex, the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely:

.
. . . .

(b)        the
right of the individual to equality before the law and the protection of the
law; ...

2.
Every law of Alberta shall, unless it is
expressly declared by an Act of the Legislature that it operates
notwithstanding the Alberta Bill of Rights, be so construed and applied as not
to abrogate, abridge or infringe or to authorize the abrogation, abridgment or
infringement of any of the rights or freedoms herein recognized and declared.

[
17
]

The IMHA made by the Province with
the Métis Settlement's General Council provides in para. 4:

This Interim Agreement does not affect, abrogate or
derogate from, or recognize or affirm any constitutional or aboriginal rights
of the Metis Settlement General Council or its members. It does not affect any
existing rights or privileges afforded in legislation, regulation or by
agreement to metis settlement members. Nothing in this Interim Agreement shall
affect, abrogate or derogate from the authority of Alberta Justice to
prosecute.

[
18
]

The IMHA made by the Province with
the Métis Nations of Alberta Association provides in para. 4:

This agreement does not affect, abrogate or derogate
from, or recognize or affirm any constitutional or aboriginal rights of the
Métis Nation of Alberta or its members. Nothing in this Interim Agreement shall
affect, abrogate or derogate from the authority of Alberta Justice to
prosecute.

[
19
]

The following paragraphs are
similar in both agreements.

Para.
(5)
Subject to any closures or
restrictions for conservation or safety purposes, a member may hunt, trap or
engage in domestic fishing (specifically, the use of nets) at all seasons of
the year, for the purposes specified in paragraph 5, on land is known as the
“Harvesting Lands”, meaning:

a)
all unoccupied provincial Crown lands in Alberta;

b)
provincial protected areas and other occupied provincial Crown lands in Alberta
that have a designation or area designated for hunting, trapping or fishing (as
the case may be);

Para.
(6)
Members may hunt, trap or engage
domestic fishing (specifically, the use of nets) on harvesting lands for
subsistence purposes. The parties agree that the occasional sharing of wildlife
or fish between members will be considered to be for subsistence purposes.

Para.
(7)
This agreement does not negate
requirements to obtain applicable licenses under Alberta legislation or
regulations governing domestic fishing (specifically, the use of nets),
commercial trapping and commercial fishing. It also does not interfere with any
legislation, regulation or agreement granting hunting or fishing rights or
privileges to members of the Metis Settlements.

Para.
(11)
Alberta will, within a
reasonable time after signing the Interim Agreement, examine all its existing harvesting
investigations prior to charges being laid where metis rights have been raised
and apply the purpose and intent of this agreement.

[
20
]

The back ground recital to the
IMHA reads:

The
parties acknowledge that there is uncertainty in the law relating to Metis
Harvesting in Alberta. The parties wish to work toward a negotiated long-term
Metis Harvesting agreement in a mutually respectful manner (the “Long Term
Agreement”). In the interim, the parties have arrived at this Interim Metis
Harvesting Agreement ( “Interim Agreement”) the parties acknowledge that the
long-term agreement may be different in form and substance from this interim
agreement.

[
21
]

Paragraph 12 of the
Natural
Resources Transfer Agreement
, 1930 (“
NRTA
”) reads:

In order to secure to the Indians of the Province the
continuance of the supply of game and fish for their support and subsistence,
Canada agrees that the laws respecting game in force in the Province from time
to time shall apply to the Indians within the boundaries thereof, provided,
however, that the said Indians shall have the right, which the Province hereby
assures to them, of hunting, trapping and fishing game and fish for food at all
seasons of the year on all unoccupied Crown lands and on any other lands to which
the said Indians may have a right of access.

[
22
]

The
Constitution Act, 1982

reads:

35.

(1)  The existing aboriginal and
treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and
affirmed.

[
23
]

The
Constitution Act, 1982

sets out the definition of “aboriginal peoples of Canada” as follows:

35.
(2)  In this Act, “aboriginal peoples of Canada”
includes the Indian, Inuit, and Métis peoples of Canada.

ANALYSIS

[
24
]

Professor Hogg, in the 4
th

edition of his text
Constitutional Law of Canada
writes at p. 1380:

A
case that is properly before a court may be capable decision on a
nonconstitutional ground or a constitutional ground or both. The course of
judicial restraint is to decide the case on the nonconstitutional ground. That
way, the dispute between the litigants is resolved, but the impact of a
constitutional decision on the powers of the legislative or executive branches
of government is avoided.

He goes on to write:

The
courts have often articulated counsels of restraint of this kind, but they have
also frequently disregarded them. If a constitutional issue has in fact been
fully argued on the basis of an adequate factual record and if the issue is
likely to recur, there is much to be said for deciding the issue then and
there, even if the case could be disposed of all nonconstitutional or narrower
constitutional basis.

[
25
]

The harvesting agreements are
interim in nature and it is my view that this is a case where a judicial ruling
on the issues raised in this case would be beneficial. It is necessary, in any
event, to consider if the IMHA can operate as a defence, as the defendant has
not established that he was exercising his aboriginal rights.

[
26
]

The Crown submits that the
defendant cannot rely on the IMHA as a defence, as Paragraph 4 of the IMHA
reserves the right to prosecute. I cannot accept this position. The agreements
provide that a Metis can hunt, trap or fish in accordance with the agreements.
Having agreed to this position, the Crown cannot validly take the position that
if a Metis does hunt ,trap or fish in that fashion, he or she can still be
prosecuted.

[
27
]

The decision of
R. v. Van Der
Peet
,
1996 CanLII 216 (SCC)
,
[1996] 2 S.C.R. 507
, establishes
that the onus is on the party
asserting the right to establish that right on a balance of probabilities.

[
28
]

The decision of
the Supreme Court
of Canada in
R. v. Powley,

2003 SCC 43 (CanLII)
,
[2003] 2 S.C.R. 207
, sets out the process to
be followed in determining a Métis rights’ issue. At para. 18 in that judgment
the court writes:

[18]      With
this in mind, we proceed to the issue of the correct test to determine the
entitlements of the Métis under
s. 35
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
. ...

(1)
Characterization of the Right

(2)
Identification of the Historic Rights‑Bearing Community

(3)
Identification of the Contemporary Rights‑Bearing Community

(4)
Verification of the Claimant’s Membership in the Relevant Contemporary
Community

(5)
Identification of the Relevant Time Frame

(6)
Determination of Whether the Practice is Integral to the Claimants’ Distinctive
Culture

(7)
Establishment of Continuity Between the Historic Practice and the Contemporary
Right Asserted

(8)
Determination of Whether or not the Right was Extinguished

(9)
If There is a Right, Determination of Whether There is an Infringement

(10)
Determination of Whether the Infringement is Justified

[
29
]

I will deal with the factors which

Powley
, supra,
indicates
should be considered.

(1)        Characterization of the Right

[
30
]

The right in question is the right
to trap in the Hinton area. The Supreme Court points out in para. 19 of the
Powley,
supra,
decision that these rights are contextual and site specific. I have
no trouble concluding that teaching his children to trap is incidental to any
aboriginal right to trap which the defendant may have.

[
31
]

There was some evidence provided
by the defendant's father that the defendant's paternal grandmother’s family
trapped west of Lac St. Anne. It was not established that his grandparents’
trapping occurred near Hinton, nor was the time frame relative to European
control of the area in which they trapped established. The court cannot make an
all inclusive determination that trapping is an aboriginal right. It must be determined
with reference to the historic and current rights bearing community. The
evidence does not establish that trapping was a part of the way of life of an
historic Métis community in this area.

(2)        Identification of the Historic Rights‑Bearing
Community

[
32
]

In para. 23 of
Powley, supra,

the Court states:

[23]      In
addition to demographic evidence, proof of shared customs, traditions, and a
collective identity is required to demonstrate the existence of a Métis
community that can support a claim to site‑specific aboriginal rights.
...

The defendant’s father gave
evidence that his mother’s parents came from Manitoba. There is no evidence of
an historic Métis community established in or around Hinton prior to the time
when Europeans effectively established political and legal control in this
particular area.

(3)        Identification of the Contemporary Rights‑Bearing
Community

[
33
]

The Supreme Court, in
Powley
,
supra,
sets out in para.
24
:

[24]      Aboriginal
rights are communal rights: They must be grounded in the existence of a
historic and present community, and they may only be exercised by virtue of an
individual’s ancestrally based membership in the present community. ...

[
34
]

I have heard evidence that there
are a number of persons of mixed aboriginal and European blood living in
Hinton. That evidence does not establish the existence of a contemporary
rights-bearing Métis community. Existence of people of mixed blood in the
community does not necessarily make that community a rights-bearing community.

In the
Powley
,
supra
, decision the Supreme Court discussed the
evidence which was capable of grounding the finding of the trial judge that Mr.
Powley had established the existence of a contemporary rights-bearing
community. This included reference to the historical evidence that much of the
original community of Sault Ste. Marie was Métis, and at the time of European
control over the area, there was continuing Métis dominance of that community.
It also takes note of the fact that the other inhabitants of that area, namely
the Indians and the Europeans, recognized the Métis as a distinct people, as
did the Métis living in that area at that time.

[
35
]

The factors considered by the
Supreme Court suggest that a rights-bearing Métis community is one which not
only self-identifies, but one which had a collective identity and perhaps some
social and political organization. It has not been established that there is a
rights bearing community in Hinton.

(4)        Verification of the Claimant's Membership
in the Relevant Contemporary Community

[
36
]

The evidence does establish that
the defendant is accepted in a contemporary Métis community in this area. There
were adjournments granted to the defendant so that he could produce a
membership card in one of the Métis organizations that is a party to the IMHA
with the Provincial Government. Despite his attempts to produce one, none was
forthcoming. The evidence does satisfy me that he was previously a member and
is a self-identifying Métis. He is an aboriginal as set out in the
Constitution
Act
. I am satisfied that he is a member of a Métis community in the Town of
Hinton. It has not been established that this community has the right to trap
in this area.

(5)        Identification of the Relevant Time Frame

[
37
]

There has been no evidence called
as to when European control was established in this area.

(6)        Determination of Whether the Practice is
Integral to the Claimants' Distinctive Culture

(7)        Establishment of Continuity Between the
Historic Practice and the Contemporary Right Asserted

[
38
]

I am satisfied that trapping is
integral to culture of the defendant and his family.

[
39
]

I am satisfied that the
defendant’s family has trapped for at least three generations and the evidence
satisfies me that there has been continuity between the historic practice and
his actions in trapping to teach his children this part of their culture. That
is not the only consideration in addressing this part of the test. The test
addresses the practice of the historic and present day Métis community. It is a
community right to which he is entitled, if he is part of a rights-bearing
community and is ancestrally connected to that community. It has not been
established that there is an historic or contemporary Métis community which has
the right to trap in this area and which has maintained this right.

(8)        Determination of Whether or not the Right
was Extinguished

(9)       If There is a Right, Determination of
Whether There is an Infringement

(10)     Determination of Whether the Infringement
is Justified

[
40
]

It is not necessary for me to
answer these questions, because of my findings with reference to the earlier
questions.

INTERIM MÉTIS HARVESTING
AGREEMENT AS A DEFENCE

[
41
]

The hunting, trapping and fishing
rights which the Métis have under the
Constitution Act, 1982
are defined
by the Supreme Court of Canada
in the decision of
R. v. Powley
,

supra
.
These are rights restricted to members of a present day Métis community with
ancestral ties to an historic Métis community in a restricted geographic area.
The IMHA purports to extend to all Métis in the province, for all areas of the
province, the rights defined by
the Supreme Court in
Powley
, supra,
It
cannot do so.

[
42
]

The provincial government has
entered into agreements with two organizations representing Métis people. There
is no constitutional status to these organizations. This is a practical
approach to working with Métis people with a view to the implementation of the
Métis aboriginal rights
considered by the Supreme Court in
Powley
,

supra
. Failure of a Métis to belong to one of these organizations does not
disentitle that Métis from the enjoyment of his constitutional rights. I am
satisfied to the extent the purpose of the IMHA is to create a process for the
implementation of Métis constitutional rights, this defendant is a person who
would be entitled to the benefit of the agreement.
The Supreme Court in
Powley
,
supra,
establishes that membership in a political organization is not
determinative of his acceptance in a contemporary Métis community.

[
43
]

I have been referred to two cases
arising in British Columbia. The first is
the case of
R. v. Huovinen

(2000),
2000 BCCA 427 (CanLII)
,
146 C.C.C. (3d) 301 (B.C.C.A.)
. This case involved the appeal of a
provincial court decision staying charges against fishermen, who are not
aboriginal, who had fished without a license at a time that the only licenses
being issued were issued to aboriginals. The British Columbia Court of Appeal
held that the prosecutions were prompted strictly by the enforcement of an
applicable law, that is closing the season to anyone who is not licensed, and
the stay was set aside. It does not address the same issues that are being
considered in this case. The
Huovinen, supra,
case was decided on the
narrow issue of whether the issuance of the license was in accordance with the
law. The British Columbia Court of Appeal chose not to look at the formulation
of the regulations in the context of the equality provisions of the
Charter
.

[
44
]

A second case is working its way
through the British Columbia judicial system.
The case of
R. v. Kapp,

2004 BCSC 958 (CanLII)
,
[2004] B.C.J. 1440 (B.C.S.C.)
is the sequel to the
Huovinen, supra,

case, with the constitutionality of the regulations upon which the Court of
Appeal hung its hat being questioned. This case is currently before the British
Columbia Court of Appeal, but regardless of the outcome it is distinguishable
from the issues before this court. It does not deal with the ability of the
minister to direct a policy which does not have a  legislative origin or to
assign special rights which are not constitutional rights.

[
45
]

The case of
R. v. Catagas

(1977),
1977 CanLII 1636 (MB CA)
,
38 C.C.C. (2d) 296
, a decision of the Manitoba Court of Appeal,
addresses similar issues to those raised in this case. Chief Justice Freedman
writes at p. 301:

So what we have here is a clear case of the exercise
of a purported dispensing power by executive action in favour of a particular
group. Such a power does not exist. The dispensation which it sought to create
was, in the words of Halsbury, “void and of no effect”.

Two points must here be noted. The first is that the
attempted dispensation was no doubt benevolent in purpose. It flowed from a
recognition of the Indian's historic right to hunt game for food at all seasons
of the year. But that was precisely the position taken by the minority judges
in the
Daniels
case. The purported dispensation would have given legal
validity to the judgment of the minority and negated the judgment of the
majority. And that of course cannot legally be done, no matter how sympathetic
one may be towards the Indians and his hunting rights.

The other point is that nothing here stated is
intended to curtail or affect the matter of prosecutorial discretion. Not every
infraction of the law, as everybody knows, results in the institution of
criminal proceedings. A wise discretion may be exercised against the setting in
motion of the criminal process. A policeman, confronting a motorist who had
been driving slightly in excess of the speed limit, may elect to give him a
warning rather than a ticket. An Attorney‑General, faced with
circumstances indicating only technical guilt of a serious offence but actual
guilt of a less serious offence, may decide to prosecute on the latter and not
on the former. And the Attorney‑General may in his discretion stay
proceedings on any pending charge, a right that is given statutory recognition
in s. 508 [am.
1972, c. 13, s. 43(1)
] and
s. 732.1
[enacted]
idem
,
s.
62
] of the
Criminal Code
. But in all these instances the prosecutorial
discretion is exercised in relation to a specific case. It is the particular
facts of a given case that call that discretion into play. But that is a far
different thing from the granting of a blanket dispensation in favour of a
particular group or race. Today the dispensing power may be exercised in favour
of Indians. Tomorrow it may be exercised in favour of Protestants, and the next
day in favour of Jews. Our laws cannot be so treated. The Crown may not by Executive
action dispense with laws. The matter is as simple as that, and nearly three
centuries of legal and constitutional history stand as the foundation for that
principle.

[
46
]

In
Catagas
, supra,
the
Manitoba Court of Appeal concluded that the Province of Manitoba could not
implement a policy that directed that applicable laws not be enforced, based on
membership in a specific group or race. In the present case we have a similar
situation, except that the position has been formalized in agreements with different
Métis organizations. The Crown has conceded that the Interim Agreements are not
legislation and are not regulation. The formalization of the policy in an
agreement cannot give it the power to override the equality rights contained in
the
Charter
or the
Alberta Bill of Rights
. The policy, and these
agreements, are not giving effect to Métis constitutional rights. Métis
hunting, trapping and fishing rights have been defined, and are restricted in
their application, by the
Powley, supra,
and
Blais,

2003 SCC 44 (CanLII)
,
[2003] 2
S.C.R. 236
decisions.

[
47
]

There is a similarity between the
manner in which the
Catagas, supra,
case and the present case developed.

In the
Catagas
, supra,
case the aboriginal community advanced the
position that an international treaty did not restrict an aboriginal’s right to
hunt migratory birds.
The Supreme Court in
Daniels v. The Queen
,
1968 CanLII 67 (SCC)
,
[1969]
1 C.C.C. 299
, ruled that it did. Notwithstanding that ruling, the Manitoba
provincial government followed a policy of continuing to permit Indians to hunt
contrary to the international treaty. In the present case, the Métis position,
taken to
the Supreme Court in
Powley
, supra
, and
Blais, supra
,
was that Métis rights were similar to Indian rights. If they were, in Alberta
any Métis would be able to exercise these rights anywhere in the province. The
Supreme Court ruled that Métis rights were more restricted than Indian rights.
In the present case, as
in
Catagas
, supra
, the provincial government has
implemented a policy, expressed by the IMHA, which ignores the ruling of the
Supreme Court and which effectively grants Métis hunting, trapping and fishing
rights which are not restricted geographically within the province and which
are not dependant on meeting the other criteria set out
in
Powley
, supra
.
It cannot do so.

[
48
]

Paragraph 12 of the
NRTA

provides that an Indian’s hunting and trapping rights can be exercised on
unoccupied Crown lands and lands in the province to which the claimant has a
right of access. The Supreme Court
decision in
R. v. Blais
,
supra
,
establishes that Métis rights have a different origin than Indian rights.
Paragraph 12 refers to Indians.
The reasoning in
Blais
, supra
, does not
permit the application of paragraph 12 to Métis.

[
49
]

The preamble to the IMHA states:

The
parties acknowledge that there is uncertainty in the law relating to Métis
harvesting in Alberta.

As a result of
the decisions
in
Powley
, supra,
and
Blais, supra
, there is no longer
uncertainty in the law as to what these rights are. There remains some
uncertainty in identifying which Métis may exercise which rights in a specific
geographic area.

[
50
]

The
Powley, supra,
decision
establishes that the exercise of an individual Métis’ rights depend on a number
of factors. Any determination of Métis aboriginal rights must also address the
issue of distinguishing those Métis who have the aboriginal right to hunt, fish
or trap in a particular area from those who do not. As the criterion are very
complex Justice Cory’s observations
in the case of
R. v. Nikal
,
1996 CanLII 245 (SCC)
,
[1996] 1
S.C.R. 1013
at para.
95
may have some application:

[95]      It
must also be remembered that aboriginal rights, by definition, can only be
exercised by aboriginal peoples. Moreover, the nature and scope of aboriginal
rights will frequently be dependant upon membership in particular bands who
have established particular rights in specific localities. In this context, a
licence may be the least intrusive way of establishing the existence of the
aboriginal right for the aboriginal person as well as preventing those who are
not aboriginals from exercising aboriginal rights.

[
51
]

For the reasons that I set out
above I conclude that the defendant cannot rely on the Interim Métis Harvesting
Agreements as a defence to this charge. He has failed to establish that he was
exercising his aboriginal rights in trapping as he did, and I convict him of
the charge. I recognize that this defendant and others may have been misled by
the actions of the province in stipulating in the Interim Métis Harvesting
Agreements that any Métis would be able to harvest wildlife anywhere in the
province. I also note that the defendant was trapping to teach his children to
trap in the tradition of his family. I impose a nominal fine in the amount of
$25.
